name: Battle of Gaugamela
info: Alexander the Great and the army of Macedon defeated the Persian army of Darius III at Gaugamela, north of Arbela in what is now Iraq, in 331 BCE; the Achaemenid Empire fell soon after.

facts.date: 1 October 331 BCE, by calculation from the lunar eclipse of 20 to 21 September of that year
facts.place: Gaugamela, a village on the river Bumodus north of Arbela (modern Erbil) in the Nineveh Plains of Iraq; the exact site is not known, and Karamlesh is the most commonly accepted
facts.sides: Alexander of Macedon with Greek allies and mercenaries (Arrian gives 7,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry, figures modern scholars generally accept) against Darius III of Persia, whose army ancient sources put at up to 1,000,000 and modern estimates at about 91,000 to 120,000, with no agreed figure
facts.outcome: Darius fled the field and the Persian army broke up; Alexander took Babylon and Darius was murdered by Bessus the next year, ending the Achaemenid Empire.

t: Ancient writers give the Persian army as up to a million men, figures modern historians call absurd or of no use; modern estimates run from about 91,000 to 120,000.
The site of the battle is not known with certainty, and the date of 1 October 331 BCE is a calculation from an eclipse reported by ancient sources.
After the battle Darius fled east and was killed by his own satrap Bessus, and the Achaemenid Empire is traditionally considered to have ended with his death.
dyk: Darius III offered Alexander all territory west of the Euphrates, his daughter in marriage and 30,000 talents of silver before the battle, according to Diodorus, Curtius and Justin; Alexander refused.
ev: Darius III loses the Battle of Issus to Alexander, who captures his wife, mother and two daughters
Alexander takes Tyre after a siege from January to July and then Gaza, and Egypt surrenders to him
Darius makes a third offer of terms, which Alexander refuses
Alexander marches from Egypt through Syria, crosses the Euphrates and then the Tigris
The armies meet at Gaugamela and Alexander leads a wedge into the Persian centre
Darius flees and Babylon is surrendered to Alexander
Bessus murders Darius, and Alexander gives him a full burial at Persepolis

sections.background:
In November 333 BCE Darius III lost the Battle of Issus to Alexander, who captured Darius's wife, his mother Sisygambis and his two daughters and gained southern Asia Minor. Alexander then besieged Tyre from January to July 332 BCE and fought at Gaza. Many Persian troops in Egypt had been withdrawn for Issus and had died there, so the satrap Mazaces surrendered Egypt peacefully.

Ancient historians give conflicting accounts of Darius's attempts to negotiate, which a modern scholar, Nawotka, calls hypothetical to reconstruct. Three attempts are usually distinguished. Darius reportedly offered to ransom his family, first for 10,000 talents, then to cede land west of the Halys river, and then to accept Alexander as co-equal. Diodorus Siculus alone says Alexander hid one letter and showed his friends a forged one. Alexander is said to have refused all offers.

The third offer, made after Alexander left Egypt, was larger: land west of the Euphrates, co-rulership, a daughter's hand and 30,000 talents. Diodorus says Parmenion advised acceptance, and Alexander answered, "So should I, if I were Parmenion." Alexander insisted there could be only one king of Asia and called on Darius to surrender or to fight. The ancient authors differ on details: Plutarch and Arrian give the ransom as 10,000 talents, the others 30,000, and Arrian places the third attempt during the siege of Tyre. Darius then prepared for another battle.
sections.forces:
Alexander commanded Greek forces from Macedon and the Hellenic League, with Greek mercenaries and levies from the tributary Paeonians and Thracians. Arrian gives 7,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry, and there is general acceptance of his numbers among modern scholars. Most historians agree that the army had 31,000 heavy infantry, including mercenaries and the allied hoplites kept in reserve, and 9,000 light infantry, mainly peltasts with some archers.

For Darius's army, modern scholars reject the ancient figures. Arrian gives 40,000 cavalry and 1,000,000 infantry, Diodorus 200,000 cavalry and 800,000 infantry, Plutarch 1,000,000 without a breakdown, and Curtius Rufus 45,000 cavalry and 200,000 infantry; Arrian, Diodorus and Curtius give 200 chariots and Arrian 15 elephants. Worthington calls these numbers absurdly high, and Bichler says the only common ground among modern authors is that they are of no use. Warry estimates 91,000, Harbottle 120,000, and Engels and Green no more than 100,000.

Most of Darius's troops were of lower quality than Alexander's. His better infantry were about 2,000 Greek mercenary hoplites and the 10,000 Immortals, and the Armenians were armed in the Greek way. He had recruited the best cavalry of the eastern satrapies and the Scythians, and had the ground levelled and cleared of bushes for his scythed chariots. Bessus commanded the left flank and Mazaeus the right, with Darius in the centre, as Persian kings traditionally did. Alexander took the right with the Companion cavalry and Parmenion the left.
sections.course:
Alexander advanced with his wings drawn back at 45 degrees to lure the Persian cavalry. While the phalanxes engaged the Persian infantry, Darius sent much of his cavalry and some infantry against Parmenion on the left, and Alexander rode to the edge of the right with his Companions, trying to draw the Persian cavalry outwards and open a gap in the centre. Darius's Scythian and Bactrian cavalry attacked Alexander's right in a long fight in which the Macedonians, greatly outnumbered, were often hard pressed; Arrian says more of Alexander's men fell there.

Darius then launched his chariots; javelin throwers stopped many, and ranks opened to let the rest pass before the hypaspists and grooms killed them. As the Persians pressed on to the flanks, Alexander formed a wedge of Companions, the guard brigade and phalanx battalions he could spare, and struck the weakened Persian centre, taking out the royal guard and the Greek mercenaries. The widely held modern view, based on Arrian, is that Darius then fled and the army followed.

Alexander did not pursue at once. Desperate messages came from Parmenion, whose wing seemed encircled by the Persian right. Alexander turned back, and Arrian describes the fiercest fighting of the day as he met Indian and Parthian cavalry and the bravest Persian division trying to break through; sixty Companions were killed. Meanwhile a gap had opened in the Macedonian line, and Persian and Indian cavalry broke through to loot the camp, where the rear phalanx dispersed them; Sisygambis refused to leave with them. Mazaeus then pulled back.
sections.aftermath:
Bagophanes formally surrendered Babylon to Alexander. Parmenion captured the Persian baggage train, and Alexander and his bodyguard pursued Darius. The booty included 4,000 talents, the king's chariot and bow, and the elephants. No casualty totals are given for either army, apart from the sixty Companions killed.

Darius escaped on horseback with a small body of men. The Bactrian cavalry and Bessus caught up with him, as did survivors of the Royal Guard and 2,000 Greek mercenaries. At that point the Persian Empire was divided into an eastern and a western half. Darius planned to go further east and raise another army, and wrote to the eastern satraps to ask them to stay loyal.

The satraps had other intentions. Bessus murdered Darius and fled east. Alexander is said to have been saddened to see an enemy he respected killed so, gave Darius a full burial at Persepolis, and pursued Bessus, whom he captured and executed the following year. Most of the remaining satraps gave their loyalty to Alexander and kept their positions. The Achaemenid Empire is traditionally considered to have ended with Darius's death.
sections.sources:
The ancient accounts are by Arrian, Diodorus Siculus, Curtius Rufus, Justin and Plutarch, writing centuries after the battle; Justin, Arrian and Curtius wrote in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. They are sometimes inconsistent and give no precise topography, so the location of the field is not known with certainty. The sites proposed include Tel Gomel, Karamlesh, Qaraqosh, Tell Aswad and a mound south of Wardak. The most commonly accepted is Karamlesh, suggested by Sir Aurel Stein in 1938; all lie in the Nineveh Plains east of Mosul and west of Erbil.

The date is a calculation. After the army crossed the Tigris a near total lunar eclipse took place on 20 to 21 September 331 BCE; four days later Alexander's men captured scouts of Mazaeus, and allowing four days' rest, the battle must have been on 1 October. The Livius.org site favours a reconstruction that relies heavily on the Babylonian astronomical diaries.

Modern historians disagree on the size of the Persian army, the numbers above, and on why Darius chose the ground. Peter Green thinks Alexander's northern route caught the Persians off guard, and that Darius, using scorched earth and scythed chariots, wanted to repeat Cunaxa; Jona Lendering argues that Darius led the Macedonians to Gaugamela on purpose, as the Persians' preferred battlefield. The episode of Parmenion's desperate messages was later used by Callisthenes and others to discredit Parmenion.
sections.legacy:
Gaugamela was the second and last battle between the two kings. It is considered to be the final blow to the Achaemenid Empire, which Alexander then conquered completely, and it is described as a decisive victory for the League of Corinth that led to the fall of Darius and of the empire. The empire was left divided into eastern and western halves when Darius fled, and the satraps who killed him were mostly allowed to keep their posts under Alexander.

The victory is credited to superior tactics and the clever use of light infantry against a much larger army. Alexander's plan of drawing the Persian cavalry to the flanks and then striking at the gap in the centre is described as an unusual strategy that has been duplicated only a few times, needing almost perfect timing. The Persian use of levelled ground and scythed chariots, by contrast, is read by Peter Green as an attempt to repeat the earlier battle of Cunaxa.

The battle has continued to be studied. Marciak and others have published work on Alexander's route to Gaugamela and Arbela, on the visibility of the battlefield, and on the battle in the Navkur Plain in the context of Macedonian and Persian warfare, and the question of the site remains open.

summary: At Gaugamela in 331 BCE Alexander of Macedon defeated Darius III of Persia, whose army ancient writers put at up to a million men and modern historians at roughly 91,000 to 120,000. Darius fled and was later murdered, and the Achaemenid Empire came to an end.
notes: The article gives no casualty totals for either side, only 60 Companions killed and three named officers wounded.

The article has no legacy or memory section, so 'legacy' rests on its lead, the tactics remarks and the further-reading list; it is the thinnest section. Nothing about later memory, art or reassessment beyond that is in the article.
The article says the Macedonian victory was 'decisive' for the League of Corinth and the 'final blow' to the Achaemenid Empire; I kept those as the article's wording and did not add a verdict.
The article says Alexander was 'saddened' at Darius's murder; I wrote 'is said to have been' and did not repeat 'respected' as fact.
Date: 1 October 331 BCE is the article's calculation from the eclipse and the four days' rest, not a date any ancient source states.
Left out: the Albanian cavalry detail, the second line's composition, the unit lists of both wings, Hannibal-free anecdotes, and the Livius site beyond a mention.
